title: Effsize - a package for efficient effect size computation
abstract: This package contains the functions to compute the standardized effect sizes for experiments (Cohen d, Hedges g, Cliff delta, Vargha and Delaney A). The computation algorithms have been optimized to allow efficient computation even with very large data sets. The package is available on the CRAN web site: http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/effsize/index.html

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

Effsize has established itself as a durable software method anchor for effect size computation, with 328 scholarly citations and 350 documented downstream reuses. Its uptake is broad and sustained, spanning articles, preprints, dissertations, and other research outputs across multiple disciplines.

Full narrative

Effsize is a software package designed to compute standardized effect sizes efficiently, including Cohen’s d, Hedges’ g, Cliff’s delta, and Vargha and Delaney’s A. The citation record shows that this functionality has been taken up as a practical methodological resource rather than a narrowly cited software note: the work has 328 citations in OpenAlex, and reuse tracking identifies 350 downstream uses.

The citing landscape suggests especially strong visibility in contemporary life-science and psychology workflows, with prominent uptake in venues such as bioRxiv, PLoS ONE, Scientific Reports, eLife, and Research Square. Most citing works are journal articles, but a substantial share are preprints, indicating that the package is being used both in established publication pipelines and in earlier-stage research dissemination.

The thematic spread of citations is also broad. While the software sits squarely in computation and statistics, it is cited across diverse research areas including psychology, ecology, microbiota research, and other empirical fields where effect size reporting matters. This cross-disciplinary reuse is consistent with the package’s role as infrastructure for routine statistical analysis rather than a domain-specific tool.

Usage and stewardship signals support this picture of sustained practical value. Zenodo records 8,303 views and 436 downloads, and the software is linked to a GitHub source repository as well as Zenodo-hosted versions. Public-discourse and event-data signals are unavailable in the current record, so the clearest evidence of impact remains the combination of citations, reuse, and distributed scholarly adoption.
